open_problems: CONFOUND (design gap): BORROW gives the model a full successful transcript, which is stronger than 'analogy'. A win may come from exposure to any worked solution, not from the borrowing. PREREG has no control arm that shows a random or wrong-scenario solved transcript, and no 'solved-example-only' arm. P2 compares X against R+ only, so it cannot separate these causes.

CONFOUND: FLIP's approach sentence is written by the same model from the same failed transcripts. Its 'opposite' is often 'ask the user first' or 'act instead of asking'. The sandbox rewards asking on ambiguous tasks, so wins may come from flipping the act-vs-ask default rather than new thinking. Logged approach texts are needed to check this, and no aggregate exists.

Shared context across tries: all 16 tries of an arm use the same 2 failed transcripts (the earliest by try_idx). Diversity comes only from sampling and the approach or borrow text. If those 2 transcripts are uninformative, every arm shares the blind spot.
FLIP coverage: if the model lists fewer than 8 assumptions, approaches repeat (try i = approach i % len). If parsing fails, all 8 tries use the same 600-char blob. Neither is reported.

BORROW transfer: tool results in the borrowed transcript are truncated at 300 chars and come from another world. The model may copy another task's tool names or arguments. Word-overlap ranking may pick similar wording rather than similar structure.

Regression to the mean: HARD = 0/64 selects tasks whose true per-try rate is low, and some of those were 0/64 by chance. Any arm with 16 tries can crack them. R+ serves as the control for this, which is why P2 is paired. The paired test uses only one sampling seed.

Replay tests reproducibility of one winning block on the same task (P3). It does not test transfer: whether the approach text cracks other HARD tasks. The playbook-card step needs a transfer test on held-out HARD tasks, which is not in PREREG.
Verdict branches: 2-4 cracked, or a gap of 1-2, is INCONCLUSIVE and needs a second seed. The PREREG does not set a seed-2 pass rule or a multiple-comparison correction across the two move types.

papers.title: Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
papers.key_idea: Coding agent that edits its own code and keeps an archive of all variants. Parent selection mixes performance with a novelty bonus that decays as a parent gets more children, so it branches from old, non-best agents too.
papers.result: SWE-bench 20.0% to 50.0%; Polyglot 14.2% to 30.7%. Authors report beating ablations without open-ended archive or self-improvement. 50% is about on par with OpenHands+CodeAct v2.1 (53.0%) per the summary.

papers.title: ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended and Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
papers.key_idea: Open-source AlphaEvolve-style loop. Three parts: exploration/exploitation parent sampling, rejection of code that is too similar (novelty filter), and a bandit that picks which LLM to call.
papers.result: Circle packing SOTA in about 150 samples; also AIME agent harness, ALE-Bench, MoE load-balance loss. Efficiency claim is the authors' framing, not a head-to-head.

papers.title: LEVI: Stronger Search Architectures Can Substitute for Larger LLMs in Evolutionary Search
papers.key_idea: CVT-MAP-Elites archive keeps diversity. A mutation router sends most edits to a small LLM and only occasional structural proposals to a big one. Rank-preserving proxy benchmark cuts rollout cost.
papers.result: Best score at 3.3-6.7x smaller budget than frontier ShinkaEvolve/GEPA/AdaEvolve runs; matches best single-problem result at 35x lower cost; matches or beats GEPA on 4 prompt tasks using under half the rollouts. Abstract fetched did not name model sizes; check the full paper before quoting small-model numbers.

papers.title: DEI: Diversity in Evolutionary Inference for Quality-Diversity Search
papers.key_idea: Distributed QD search with heterogeneous LLM ensembles, diversified across model families rather than only sizes.
papers.result: Diverse ensemble beats solo model and homogeneous ensemble on archive coverage (per search summary; not read in full).

papers.title: Heuresis: Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents Across Quality, Diversity and Novelty
papers.key_idea: Compares six search strategies (Greedy, MAP-Elites, Go-Explore, Islands, Curiosity, Omni) for LLM agents that propose and run ML experiments, scoring quality, embedding diversity and web-checked novelty.
papers.result: 3,222 scored runs. No idea rated fully original (best was minor similarity). Greedy best on nanoGPT; MAP-Elites best on MinAtar RL. Only one novel-leaning idea in top 10 by quality. Agents fabricated results in 40 of 1,628 audited runs. Directly relevant to sandbox-only writes and checking.

papers.title: FlowRL: Matching Reward Distributions for LLM Reasoning
papers.key_idea: GFlowNet-style: turn rewards into a normalized target distribution with a learned partition function, then minimize reverse KL, so the policy keeps less-frequent valid solutions instead of collapsing to the top one.
papers.result: About +10.0% over GRPO and +5.1% over PPO on math (abstract). Solution diversity reportedly about doubles (ICLR slides). Tested on 7B-scale reasoning, not on tool-use or small nightly-trained models.

papers.title: Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
papers.key_idea: Training-free prompt: ask the model for k candidates with probabilities, so it is not pushed to the single typical answer. Mode collapse is blamed on typicality bias in preference data.
papers.result: Creative-writing diversity 1.6-2.1x over direct prompting (per summary; not verified). Cheap first step for the FLIP/BORROW arms, which can be tested with no training.

papers.title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
papers.key_idea: Agentic tree search with an experiment-manager agent, no human code templates, and a VLM feedback loop on figures.
papers.result: Three autonomous manuscripts sent to an ICLR workshop; one passed the average human acceptance bar. Pruning-by-novelty detail came only from a blog, unverified.

papers.title: LLMatic: Neural Architecture Search via Large Language Models and Quality Diversity Optimization
papers.key_idea: LLM as mutation operator inside two QD archives; model complexity used as a diversity descriptor.
papers.result: Early evidence that QD archives plus LLM mutation work; older, so it sets the baseline rather than the frontier.

gaps_nobody_solved: No paper I found runs QD/MAP-Elites or novelty archives on a 3-4B model that is also fine-tuned nightly with a KL anchor. LEVI is closest but uses a small LLM only as a mutation operator and is not a nightly learner.

Nobody has shown that the search archive's best finds can be distilled back into weights (the sleep step) without losing diversity. FlowRL keeps diversity during RL but was not tested in an archive-plus-distill loop.

Mode-as-operator is untested: FLIP (change the hidden assumption) and BORROW (analogy) as explicit diversity operators inside one model, judged by checkers in a tool sandbox. Verbalized Sampling and DGM each cover only part of this.
Greedy decoding as the bottleneck for small models is not addressed in these papers. Heuresis reports Greedy winning on one task, which argues against assuming diversity search always beats greedy.
Fabricated-result rate (40/1,628 in Heuresis) means any creative loop needs a hard external checker. No method above showed how to keep that checker honest when the model writes its own tasks.
No 2025-2026 paper I found benchmarks evolutionary search on hard tool-use tasks with a 0/64 plain-try baseline. Reach-1 would be a new kind of test bed.
FunSearch and AlphaEvolve were not checked in this sweep (search returned only secondary mentions), so their ids are not in this list. Verify before citing their numbers.

papers.title: ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
papers.key_idea: Distills reusable reasoning strategies from both successful AND failed agent attempts into a memory bank; retrieved at test time; MaTTS (memory-aware test-time scaling) generates varied trajectories to give contrastive signal.
papers.result: Reported to beat raw-trajectory and success-only memory on web-browsing and SWE benchmarks, with higher success and fewer steps. Snippets only; numbers not verified.

papers.title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
papers.key_idea: Context as an evolving playbook via Generator / Reflector / Curator, no weight updates; names brevity bias and context collapse as failure modes.
papers.result: Reported +10.6% on agent benchmarks, +8.6% on finance vs strong baselines. Small-model evaluation not confirmed from sources.

papers.title: GFlowRL: Scaling Distribution-Matching RL to Large Language Models
papers.key_idea: GFlowNet-style reward-distribution matching with in-batch Monte Carlo partition estimate (no extra network), importance-sampling correction and flow-gap clipping; keeps diverse high-reward paths instead of mode-collapsing.
papers.result: Abstract-level claims: beats counterparts on math, code, red-teaming; Codeforces 2048 at 14B; top ASR on AdvBench/HarmBench. FlowRL diverges on red-teaming and fails to converge on MoE. Models 14B dense and MoE up to 235B. Not a small-model result.

papers.title: GFlowNet Fine-tuning for Diverse Correct Solutions in Mathematical Reasoning Tasks
papers.key_idea: Train output distribution proportional to reward so diverse correct intermediate reasoning steps are kept; compared with reward-max RL.
papers.result: Reported more diverse correct solutions than reward-max baseline on math; numbers not fetched.

papers.title: Universe of Thoughts: Enabling Creative Reasoning with Large Language Models
papers.key_idea: Formalizes combinational (cross-domain transfer), exploratory (search within concept space) and transformational (change the space's governing rules/constraints) creativity as operators; variants C-UoT, E-UoT, T-UoT. Closest to Ben's FLIP (transformational) and BORROW (combinational) arms.
papers.result: HypoArena (Qwen3-14B): E-UoT pairwise win 32.7% vs 25.5% next best (7 methods). GPT-4o on Bridge/Electricity/Society tasks; no baseline numbers on creative tasks in fetched page. Metrics named feasibility/utility/novelty in earlier search snippet, not confirmed on abstract page.

papers.title: Enhancing Structural Mapping with LLM-derived Abstractions for Analogical Reasoning in Narratives (YARN)
papers.key_idea: LLM decomposes narratives into units, abstracts them at four levels, then a structural mapping engine aligns elements across stories (fixes cognitive mapping engines needing pre-extracted entities). Abstract-then-instantiate analogy pipeline.
papers.result: Abstract says abstractions consistently improve performance and are competitive with or better than end-to-end LLM baselines; no figures fetched.

papers.title: Mechanistic study of LLM relational-concept encoding and transfer
papers.key_idea: Probes whether LLMs encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to new entities; finds limited transfer; activation patching at key token positions partly transfers information.
papers.result: Qualitative; limited transfer to new entities. Not fetched, from snippet only.

papers.title: No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
papers.key_idea: Negative-result study: 280 participants; LLM use did not improve quality of problem frames. Counterweight to any claim that LLM reframing helps.
papers.result: No measurable improvement in frame quality from LLM use.

papers.title: Igniting Creative Writing in Small Language Models: LLM-as-a-Judge versus Multi-Agent Refined Rewards
papers.key_idea: RLAIF on a 7B SLM for creative generation; compares a reward model from multi-agent rejection sampling vs principle-guided LLM-as-judge with adversarial/reflection tuning. Shows SFT limits novelty.
papers.result: Both reward strategies significantly improve creative output over baselines; principle-guided judge best; cheaper training and less human data. Only a 7B model; closest small-model creativity-reward analog.

papers.title: Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
papers.key_idea: Model selects atomic reasoning modules (e.g. step-back, critical thinking) and composes a task-specific reasoning structure before answering.
papers.result: Up to +32% vs CoT on BBH/MATH-type tasks; >20% over CoT-self-consistency at 10-40x less inference compute (per abstract).

papers.title: Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (Step-Back Prompting)
papers.key_idea: Abstract the question to high-level principles first, then reason from them; step-back as a prompting move.
papers.result: PaLM-2L: +7% MMLU Physics, +11% Chemistry, +27% TimeQA, +7% MuSiQue (per snippet). Older than 2025; no 2025-26 follow-up surfaced.

papers.title: BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for LLMs
papers.key_idea: Benchmark that requires defying default commonsense associations; lateral-thinking puzzles with puzzle variations to test consistency.
papers.result: Substantial gap between SOTA LLMs and humans; inconsistent answers across variations. Good test-bed to borrow for HARD-task style checks.

papers.title: uTeBC-NLP at SemEval-2024 Task 9: Can LLMs be Lateral Thinkers?
papers.key_idea: Compares CoT, direct, and RAG prompting on BRAINTEASER sentence puzzles.
papers.result: Small-scale shared-task entry; minor relevance.

gaps_nobody_solved: No 2025-26 paper found that trains a 3-4B model nightly (LoRA plus KL anchor) to switch into a creative mode that changes the problem, with playbook cards then weights; ReasoningBank and ACE are inference-time memory, not weight-level creative modes.
Few sources test whether reframing (FLIP/BORROW) helps greedy-decoding small models; the one negative study (2503.01631) is human-facing, and UoT results are on GPT-4o and Qwen3-14B only.
Diversity-preserving RL (GFlowRL, Takase GFlowNet) is validated at 14B and above or on math; no evidence found at 3-4B or on tool-use sandboxes with checkable rewards, which is Reach-1's setting.

Greedy-decoding bottleneck: no retrieved paper addresses making first-try sampling reproduce search-found fits via training; GFlowNet diversity claims are not tested against pass@1 on a fixed-budget hard split.
Automatic judging of novelty without an LLM judge is unsolved in these sources; ACE and UoT rely on judges or win rates.
Searches surfaced no 2026 small-model step-back or self-discover follow-up; the 2023-24 originals are the only evidence.
Verify claims before relying on them: GFlowRL and YARN results were read from abstracts only; ACE small-model use and UoT novelty metrics were not confirmed from full text.

papers.title: STARS: Stiefel-based Activation Steering for Diverse Reasoning (ICLR 2026)
papers.key_idea: Training-free. At each token, steer the hidden activations of several concurrent generation runs with additive directions chosen to maximize the geometric volume of the steered activations. The Stiefel constraint keeps the directions orthogonal, pushing runs onto different trajectories. Uses a one-step Riemannian update with closed-form stepsize for real-time use.
papers.result: Abstract only (fetched): claims more diversity than standard sampling with no quality loss on test-case generation and scientific discovery. Model sizes and numbers not retrieved. Treat as unverified until the PDF is read.

papers.title: Noise Steering for Controlled Text Generation: Improving Diversity and Reading-Level Fidelity in Arabic Educational Story Generation (BEA 2026)
papers.key_idea: Training-free. Add calibrated Gaussian noise to internal representations at inference. Compares residual-stream noise, attention-logit noise (unstable alone), and AENI, an attention-entropy variant that stabilizes it. Baseline is high-temperature sampling.
papers.result: Qualitative only (abstract): residual-stream noise raised narrative diversity with little loss in quality or constraint adherence and kept reading level. High temperature inflated reading grade and collapsed on several models. Five 7-9B Arabic-centric models, small scope, no numbers retrieved.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Innovators: latent-space exploration for novelty (v2: Geometry of Knowledge Allows Extending Diversity Boundaries of LLMs)
papers.key_idea: No weights changed. Traverse the semantic/embedding space of ideas, build a conditioning distribution from a few diverse anchor generations (interpolate and perturb), and feed it in through an xRAG-style projector as a continuous token. Argues VAE-style priors fit clustered LLM semantic geometry poorly. v1 used a Mistral 7B decoder with GPT-4o as judge.
papers.result: Abstract claims substantial diversity gains, evaluated on NoveltyBench and AUT per search snippets. No numbers verified from the fetched page. Check the v2 HTML for numbers.

papers.title: Wu et al., seed-conditioning / input-layer noise for open-ended creativity (ICML 2025 spotlight)
papers.key_idea: Inject noise at the input layer (seed-conditioning) to get randomness. Frames it as a minimal testbed for open-ended creativity.
papers.result: Reported in search snippet only: input-layer noise works about as well as output-temperature sampling and sometimes better, without hurting coherence. Not fetched.

papers.title: Verbalized Sampling (mode collapse from preference data)
papers.key_idea: Argues annotators favor familiar text, so the collapse is partly in the data. Training-free prompting asks the model to verbalize a distribution over responses and samples from it.
papers.result: Snippet only. Training-free and cheap, so usable on a 3.7B model. Already in known-ids.

papers.title: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning is Designed to Mode Collapse (introduces Mode Anchored Reward Augmentation, MARA)
papers.key_idea: Argues KL-regularized RL has unimodal optima by design. Proposes MARA to change the reward so training keeps several modes.
papers.result: Snippet only (alphaXiv summary). Relevant to the KL-anchored nightly LoRA: the KL anchor may itself drive collapse.

papers.title: GFlowRL: Scaling Distribution-Matching RL to Large Language Models (Microsoft Research)
papers.key_idea: GFlowNet-style distribution matching for LLM RL. Samples in proportion to reward instead of maximizing it.
papers.result: Snippet only. Date inferred from the ID. Closest match to the FlowRL/GFlowNet re-sharing idea. Related: 2504.19981 (PRM-guided step-level GFlowNets, Llama3.2-3B, +2.59 points on MATH L5, not in known-ids).

papers.title: Want Better Synthetic Data? Steer It: Activation Steering for Low-Resource Language Generation
papers.key_idea: Activation steering for synthetic data. Early-layer steering raised diversity and often helped downstream results. Deeper-layer quality steering could reduce diversity.
papers.result: Snippet only. Layer choice matters: early-layer steering for diversity, deep-layer for quality.

papers.title: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights for Divergent Thinking (uncertain identity)
papers.key_idea: Data-free contrastive weight steering to raise divergent thinking. The closest thing to baking a creative mode into weights.
papers.result: Snippet only: up to +14 human percentile points on the Divergent Association Task, and a 720-person human study with gains in originality and surprise. Search results gave conflicting titles for this ID (one alphaXiv page called it an intro to divergent thinking and the Artificial Hivemind), so verify before citing.

papers.title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond) (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.key_idea: Defines intra-model repetition and inter-model homogeneity. Introduces Infinity-Chat (26K open-ended queries, 6 top-level categories, 17 subcategories) and 31,250 human annotations. Finds reward models and LM judges poorly calibrated to idiosyncratic human preferences.
papers.result: Diagnostic benchmark, not a fix. Warns that ensembles may not add diversity when members share alignment priors. Already in known-ids.

papers.title: Diverse, not Short: Length-Controlled Data Selection for Response Diversity (EMNLP 2025)
papers.key_idea: Self-learning on about 3,000 length-controlled preference pairs. Smaller models (Olmo-2-7B) act as diversity teachers for larger ones.
papers.result: Snippet only. Tested on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Olmo-2. Closest data-side method for nightly training, not verified at 3B.

gaps_nobody_solved: No verified results for latent or activation-space diversity at 3-4B on tool-use or multistep tasks. Almost every method found was tested at 7-9B or larger, or on creative writing rather than agent tasks.
No work on whether activation-noise or steering diversity survives a KL-anchored nightly LoRA update, or whether it undoes RLHF mode collapse in a model that keeps learning.

No method found that turns an inference-time creative steering vector into a weight-level mode that a nightly process can train and keep, while still measuring success on verifiable tool tasks. CreativityNeuro is the nearest and its identity is uncertain.

Little evidence that more diverse samples turn into better solutions on verifiable tasks. Most diversity papers measure novelty or diversity scores, not pass rates on hard tasks where plain tries get 0 of 64.

Greedy decoding bottleneck (from Ben's notes) has no latent-space fix found here. STARS and noise steering change the sampling distribution but do not show search over latent states finding solutions first-try decoding misses.
Layer choice for diversity versus quality is open (2606.18389 says early layers for diversity, deep layers for quality), and no sweep for small models was found.
Test-harness gap: NoveltyBench and AUT are not the same as the Reach-1 checker. Nobody has shown a creativity-mode gain on a sandbox with objective checks.
Search coverage: one search was left unused, and no full-text reads were done for STARS, noise steering, or 2507.13874 numbers. Verify the numbers before using them in a design decision.

papers.title: Meta-RL Induces Exploration in Language Agents (LaMer, ICLR 2026)
papers.key_idea: Cross-episode meta-RL: trains agents to explore across episodes and optimize long-term reward, with in-context policy adaptation via reflection on task feedback (no gradient updates at test time).
papers.result: Abstract reports +11% Sokoban, +14% MineSweeper, +19% WebShop over RL baselines, plus better generalization to harder or unseen tasks. Model sizes not stated in abstract (the search snippet names Qwen3-4B).

papers.title: MAGE: Meta-RL for Language Agents toward Strategic Exploration and Exploitation
papers.key_idea: Extends meta-RL to multi-agent settings: agent must adapt to opponents across episodes; multi-episode training plus population-based training.
papers.result: Reported to generalize to unseen opponents. Only abstract/snippet read; no numbers checked.

papers.title: Agent RL via Pivotal-Aware Self-Feedback Retry (PivoARL)
papers.key_idea: Structured self-reflection finds the pivotal erroneous turn in a failed trajectory; retry locally from that state, reusing the correct prefix; credit assignment rewards correct prefixes and isolates erroneous suffixes.
papers.result: Avg ~11.5% Pass@2/3 gain over MetaRL across 4 agent tasks and 7 search QA benchmarks; Minesweeper beats GiGPO by >45% and cuts turns ~42% vs full-retry. Model sizes not stated.

papers.title: Reflective Recovery: Self-Supervised Reasoning by Learning from Mistakes
papers.key_idea: Keep the initial segments of failed reasoning traces, concatenate with the prompt, and train on them so the model learns to recognize and correct its own early errors without critics or reward models.
papers.result: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: AIME 2025 30.0 to 37.5%; Minerva 37.6 to 47.8%. Only 7B tested in what was read; the 'Scaling Collapse' claim has no figures in the fetched text.

papers.title: Jointly Reinforcing Diversity and Quality in Language Model Generations (DARLING)
papers.key_idea: RL reward multiplies quality by a learned semantic-partition diversity score (average pairwise distance within the group), so diversity is optimized beyond lexical variation.
papers.result: Claims higher quality and novelty than quality-only RL on non-verifiable tasks; on competition math, higher pass@1 and pass@k. A third-party review flags a sign error in the core reward, unverified by me.

papers.title: Pass@k Training for Adaptively Balancing Exploration and Exploitation of Large Reasoning Models
papers.key_idea: Uses pass@k as the RL reward with an analytic advantage estimate to cut variance; aims to raise pass@k while keeping pass@1.
papers.result: Reported to improve pass@k while maintaining pass@1 vs pass@1 training. A separate 2511.16231 paper argues pass@k is a diagnostic, not an objective. Numbers not read.

papers.title: Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-play Reasoning with Zero Data
papers.key_idea: One model proposes and solves its own verifiable code/math tasks; learning from self-generated, executor-checked problems with no human data.
papers.result: Foundational self-play baseline; numbers not read.

papers.title: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM
papers.key_idea: Challenger and Solver roles from one base model co-evolve under RL to generate harder problems.
papers.result: Numbers not read.

papers.title: G-Zero: Self-Play for Open-Ended Generation from Zero Data
papers.key_idea: Intrinsic reward Hint-delta: predictive shift between unassisted response and response conditioned on a self-generated hint, for non-verifiable generation.
papers.result: Search snippet only; numbers not read.

papers.title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning
papers.key_idea: Self-play style generation of hard math problems checked by a verifier, targeting difficulty rather than novelty.
papers.result: Search snippet only.

papers.title: Endogenous Exploration in RL with Intrinsic Curiosity
papers.key_idea: Curiosity-driven exploration via a Liquid State Machine substrate.
papers.result: Not LLM work; tested on LunarLander and BipedalWalker. Included only as a curiosity reference.

papers.title: Expanding LLM Agent Boundaries with Strategy-Guided Exploration
papers.key_idea: Strategy-guided exploration to extend what LLM agents can solve.
papers.result: Only seen as a reference in search; not read.

gaps_nobody_solved: No result tests a 3-4B local model that learns nightly from its own logs with a KL anchor; all method numbers come from 7B+ models or are unstated.

Mode switching (a creative/exploration mode of the same model triggered by stuck signals such as repeated tool errors) has no matching paper found; the closest are LaMer's reflection loop and PivoARL's retry-from-pivot.

Changing the problem (flip a hidden assumption, borrow by analogy) as an exploration operator in an RL loop is not covered by the pass@k, DARLING, or self-play papers, which diversify answers or generate new problems but do not reframe a failed task.
Learning from near misses as a reusable card library that later becomes weights is not found; PivoARL and Reflective Recovery reuse failed prefixes only within the same task.

Pass@k is contested as a training reward (one paper calls it a diagnostic only), so a clear test of whether exploration gains survive greedy decoding is open. This matches the known greedy-decoding bottleneck.
Few results measure transfer from a training sandbox to held-out tool tasks at small scale, which is what Reach-1 needs.

papers.title: AgentHER: Hindsight Experience Replay for LLM Agent Trajectory Relabeling
papers.key_idea: Offline. Failed trajectories are relabeled to a goal they did achieve (LLM-guided, confidence-gated), then packaged as SFT/DPO data. Relabels only the goal and keeps the trajectory fixed.
papers.result: Reported in abstract: about +7 to +12 points over success-only SFT on WebArena and ToolBench, across four model families, about 2x data efficiency. Taken from abstracts, not the full paper.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Online Learning in LM Agents via Hindsight Trajectory Rewriting
papers.key_idea: Hu, Van Durme, Andreas, Jhamtani. Online, prompt-based. The LM rewrites failed trajectories (goal and steps) into optimized trajectories for alternative goals and keeps compressed versions in memory. More expressive than goal-only HER.
papers.result: Up to 80% over vanilla LM agents on XMiniGrid and PeopleJoinQA. On XMiniGrid it beats Reflexion and AWM. Memory-based, no weight updates.

papers.title: LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
papers.key_idea: Wake-sleep style library learning. The LLM synthesizes code, Stitch compresses it into abstractions, and an LLM auto-documents them so later prompts can use them. Adding raw abstractions to the prompt hurt; documentation fixed that.
papers.result: Beats DreamCoder by +33.14 on REGEX and +20.42 on LOGO (paper). DreamCoder search took more than two CPU-months per domain.

papers.title: ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions
papers.key_idea: Gradient-free. A frozen LLM refactors its own code into shared helper functions, and each edit is checked by execution.
papers.result: CodeLlama-13B: +11.5% LOGO, +26.1% date understanding, +8.1% TextCraft (paper).

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Self-Improving Agent with Skill Library
papers.key_idea: Skill Augmented GRPO. Agents run chains of similar tasks so skills from earlier tasks enter a library for later ones; a skill-integrated reward is added to outcome reward. Puts Voyager-style skill libraries into RL training.
papers.result: AppWorld, on an SFT model: +8.9% scenario goal completion, 26% fewer steps, 59% fewer tokens. The SFT stage uses expert traces generated by Claude, so the setup is not from-scratch. Code is for academic use only.

papers.title: ToolLibGen: Scalable Automatic Tool Creation and Aggregation for LLM Reasoning
papers.key_idea: Generated tools that fail are sent back with the full failed trajectory for revision. Tools that work get added to a toolset and aggregated.
papers.result: Not checked in detail. Search summary only; no numbers gathered.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Tool Makers
papers.key_idea: A strong model makes tools, and a lighter model uses them. Caches tools for reuse, which cuts cost.
papers.result: Not checked in this sweep. Foundational.

papers.id_or_url: arXiv 2606.03979 (Language Models Need Sleep, one of two sleep papers)
papers.title: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories
papers.key_idea: Alternates wake and sleep. A dreaming phase proposes synthetic examples, ranks them by fine-tuning gradient, and keeps those that improve task performance. Distills short-term memory into long-term parameters.
papers.result: Not verified. Secondary summary only (hyper.ai). Sources disagree on which 'Language Models Need Sleep' ID is which paper, so check both IDs before citing.

papers.id_or_url: arXiv 2605.26099 (Language Models Need Sleep, second paper)
papers.title: Language Models Need Sleep (fast-weight consolidation version, title as reported)
papers.key_idea: Offline recurrent passes write recent context into fast weights in SSM blocks before the KV cache is cleared. Aimed at long-horizon reasoning, not failure replay.
papers.result: Not verified.

papers.title: Learning Abstractions for Hierarchical Planning in Program-Synthesis Agents
papers.key_idea: The agent learns its own abstractions, writing PDDL files with in-context learning, and grows a skill library over successive environments.
papers.result: Not checked in detail.

papers.title: Prospective Compression in Human Abstraction Learning
papers.key_idea: An LLM is used as a comparison model for library learning. It writes Python helpers and refines them over up to five iterations, with DSL primitives given as context.
papers.result: Not checked in detail. Uses GPT-5.2 as backend.

papers.id_or_url: arXiv 2607.08010 (Tool-Making and Self-Evolving LLM Agents in Low-Latency Systems)
papers.title: Tool-Making and Self-Evolving LLM Agents in Low-Latency Systems
papers.key_idea: Compiles repeated procedural steps into validated tools and repairs candidate tools against labeled cases.
papers.result: Not checked. Aimed at production systems, not small models.

papers.id_or_url: ACL 2026 critique: Is This LLM Library Learning? (Berlot-Attwell, Sesterhenn, Rudzicz, Si)
papers.title: Is This LLM Library Learning? Evaluation Must Account For Compute and Behaviour
papers.key_idea: Argues that gains from caching generated tools without finetuning are not as large as they look. Evaluation must count compute and behaviour, not only task score.
papers.result: Abstract only, not checked for its numbers. Use as a caution for any tool-cache claim.

gaps_nobody_solved: Nothing found checks library learning or tool creation on 3-4B local models over repeated nightly cycles. The published numbers are mostly 13B+ or GPT-class models.
No paper found that tests incubation: offline replay of failures that produces a later insight, measured on a fixed hard set.

AgentHER and ECHO relabel for goals that were reached, which gives positive examples. None of the found work uses a flip or borrow operator to change the problem itself on failed tasks, which is the Premonition FLIP and BORROW idea.
SAGE and AgentHER both need a stronger model or a teacher for relabeling or SFT traces (Claude in SAGE). A local-only version with no API has not been shown.
Compute-matched comparisons of skill libraries against plain resampling with the same budget. The ACL 2026 critique suggests many library-learning gains disappear under that control.

The known-ids check says ECHO (2510.10304), SAGE (2512.17102), TheoryCoder-2 (2602.00929), the Prospective Compression paper (2605.09985), ToolLibGen (2510.07768) and LoopTool (2511.09148) are not in known-ids. Check those first when deciding what to add.
Sleep-style consolidation papers from 2026 disagree on which arXiv ID carries which title. Verify both before citing either.

papers.title: NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity
papers.key_idea: Groups sampled responses into functional-equivalence classes; distinct_k counts unique classes among k samples; utility_k combines novelty and quality, counting only novel generations and discounting by user patience (p=0.8). Prompts span randomness, factual knowledge, creativity and subjectivity; 100 prompts have 8 human annotators.
papers.result: Across 20 leading LLMs, diversity is well below human writers. Larger models within a family are often less diverse than smaller ones. In-context regeneration prompts help, but the distributional gap remains. Reported in abstract; numbers not verified in full text.

papers.title: Beyond Divergent Creativity: A Human-Based Evaluation of Creativity in LLMs (Nakajima, Zuiderveld, Pezzelle)
papers.key_idea: Argues the Divergent Association Task (embedding distance between 10 nouns) mostly measures novelty and ignores appropriateness. Proposes Conditional DAT (CDAT), which scores novelty conditional on contextual appropriateness.
papers.result: Several SOTA LLMs score below a random baseline and a task-aware baseline on DAT. Shows the embedding-distance proxy can reward randomness.

papers.title: Rethinking Creativity Evaluation: A Critical Analysis of Existing Creativity Evaluations
papers.key_idea: Audits LLM-based creativity judges and proposes jointly assessing novelty and acceptability rather than novelty alone.
papers.result: Reports LLM judges are only marginally better than random on creative writing (from search snippet; not verified in full text).

papers.title: Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks (COLM 2026)
papers.key_idea: Scores agent trajectories on P-Creativity (novelty vs the agent's own prior solutions), H-Creativity (novelty vs human solutions) and usefulness, using a GPT-5 judge with a 0-4 rubric.
papers.result: LLM judge reportedly correlates strongly with humans. Agents explore novel regions, but P-Creativity declines from exploration to exploitation, and the novelty does not convert into better task performance.

papers.title: Automated Creativity Evaluation of Language Models Across Open-Ended Tasks
papers.key_idea: Reference-free novelty via semantic entropy, benchmarked against human annotations and LLM novelty judgments; multi-agent LLM judging framework for task fulfilment.
papers.result: Abstract-level only; figures not verified.

papers.title: Why Large Language Models and Humans Converge and Diverge in Evaluating Creativity
papers.key_idea: Compares six LLMs with human creativity judgments across dimensions.
papers.result: LLMs agree most with humans on novelty and diverge most on contextual factors (market and reputational information). Abstract-level only.

papers.title: FlowRL: Matching Reward Distributions for LLM Reasoning (ICLR 2026)
papers.key_idea: Replaces reward maximization with matching a normalized reward-derived target distribution, via a learnable partition function and reverse-KL minimization, so rarer valid reasoning paths keep probability mass. Adds length normalization and importance sampling for variable-length CoT.
papers.result: Reported +10.0% over GRPO and +5.1% over PPO on math benchmarks, plus a diversity analysis showing more diverse solution exploration. Numbers from secondary summaries.

papers.title: GFlowNet Fine-tuning for Diverse Correct Solutions in Mathematical Reasoning Tasks (Takase et al.)
papers.key_idea: Applies GFlowNet fine-tuning so the LLM samples correct solutions roughly in proportion to reward, instead of concentrating on one mode.
papers.result: Comparable accuracy to RL baselines (no significant difference) but significantly more distinct correct solutions.

papers.title: Flow of Reasoning: Efficient Training of LLM Policy with Divergent Thinking (Yu et al.)
papers.key_idea: Treats multi-step LLM reasoning as a Markovian flow; the policy samples reasoning paths with probability proportional to unnormalized reward.
papers.result: With about 15 training examples, finds diverse high-quality solutions on BlocksWorld, Game24 and PrOntoQA (from abstract).

papers.title: Project Aletheia
papers.key_idea: Verifier-guided distillation trains a 7B model to detect contradictions and backtrack, arguing latent self-verification emerges in small models.
papers.result: Focused on constraint-satisfaction reasoning, not creative generation. Snippet-level only.

papers.title: Heuresis (research-agent search primitives)
papers.key_idea: Abstracts the research pipeline into composable primitives for open-ended exploration, scoring quality, diversity and novelty together as search objectives.
papers.result: Framework paper; no numbers pulled from snippet.

papers.title: Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
papers.key_idea: MAP-Elites with LLM variation operators and LLM scoring of quality and diversity for subjective text domains.
papers.result: Background precedent for an LLM as evaluator inside an archive.

papers.title: Large Language Models as In-context AI Generators for Quality-Diversity
papers.key_idea: LLM reads current archive elites as few-shot context and proposes new candidates for archive insertion.
papers.result: Reported to usually beat plain MAP-Elites at finding high-fitness regions (from snippet).

gaps_nobody_solved: No found paper pairs an explicit LLM novelty judge with a MAP-Elites or archive-based search over a tool-use task; the closest are QDAIF and in-context QD, and both are text or art domains, not agent recovery.

Usefulness-conditioned novelty for 3-4B local models: the judge papers (2601.20546, 2508.05470, 2607.22218) use GPT-5 or frontier judges; no validated small-judge (under ~7B) for novelty-with-appropriateness was found.
Novelty that converts into task success: 2608.30047 finds agents explore novel regions but do not turn novelty into performance; no method found that closes that gap.
Nightly-learning loops: no found work trains a small model on its own novel-and-accepted outputs over repeated nights with a KL anchor, so the sleep-to-weights step for creative wins is unaddressed.

Greedy-decoding bottleneck (search finds fits first-try never reproduces) is not addressed by the diversity papers found, which measure diversity but not whether diverse samples are reachable at pass@1.
Reach-1 style checkable tool tasks: diversity papers use human or LLM judges for novelty; no found work uses a deterministic checker for usefulness and a separate novelty metric in the same loop.
Search results were snippet-level; only 8 web searches were used and no page fetches, so all numbers beyond the abstracts are unverified.

candidates.name: Check-Lexicase Stepping-Stone Archive (Go-Explore over partial wins)
candidates.one_line: Keep every failed try that passed a different subset of checks as an elite in a persistent per-task archive. Pick parents by lexicase selection over checks, then either return to a parent's exact sandbox state and continue, or cross two parents whose partial wins complement each other. A 0/64 task gets cracked by recombining specialists, not by resampling from scratch.
candidates.mechanism:
STORED: one JSON archive per task (about 2-20 KB). Cell key = (bitvector of end-state checks passed, sorted set of tool names used, asked-vs-acted flag). Each cell holds its best elite, ranked by checks passed and then by fewer turns: the transcript, the tool-call list, and a 40-token 'what this try was going for' note written by the model. A failed try that passes 3 of 5 checks gets its own cell. R+ throws exactly those tries away.
GENERATIONS (nights; also usable live): gen 0 = 8 plain tries seed the archive. Gens 1-3 each make 8 children. (1) Lexicase parent selection: shuffle the task's checks, keep the elites that pass check 1, then of those the ones that pass check 2, and so on, and pick at random among the survivors. A specialist that alone passes a rare check is picked often; an all-round mediocre try is not. (2) Two operators, half the children each. RETURN: deterministically replay the parent's tool-call prefix in the sandbox up to the step where its last newly-passing check became true, then let the model continue from that real world state, with the still-failing checks named (check name or docstring). CROSS: take two parents whose check vectors are complementary (their union passes more checks than either one), show both transcripts and their pass/fail lists, and ask for one attempt that keeps A's achievements and adds B's. (3) Score each child with the same checks. It is inserted if it opens a new cell or beats a cell's elite. The task is cracked when any child passes all checks. The success gate stays all-checks, so partial credit only shapes which tries are kept, never what counts as a success. That avoids the reward-shaping that caused say-instead-of-do.
ACROSS NIGHTS: the archive persists, so a task Ben hit on Monday starts Tuesday from its stepping stones. A crack becomes a playbook-card candidate: its note plus the parent lineage. MODEL PARTS: no weight change. K2 plays proposer, continuer and crosser through prompts. The existing card/LoRA morning step is the only training.
REAL-USE ANALOG of the per-check bits: tool-error types, Ben's 'that part is right but X is wrong', and the nightly stuck-low task checks.
candidates.why_fantastic: Every creative arm so far (R+, FLIP, BORROW, dream school) restarts from scratch and keeps only full successes. In that regime a 0/64 task stays at 0. Open-ended evolution works because it keeps stepping stones that are different but not yet good. Lexicase selection is known in genetic programming to protect specialists better than average-fitness selection. Go-Explore's return-then-explore is what cracked hard-exploration games, and a deterministic sandbox makes the return exact and free. Partial check credit turns a flat 0/1 into a map of niches. The creative mode becomes a memory of how close it got and in which directions, and that memory compounds night over night. This is a different kind of search, not a better resample.
candidates.why_new: Not in the tried or queued list. R+, FLIP and BORROW are single-generation and keep only successes. Blocks and composition chain whole successful programs, while this recombines partial failures. Hindsight relabel changes the goal, while this keeps the goal and keeps the partial try. Aha/MDL picks among one model's proposals in one round. Literature: Go-Explore uses pixel or state cells, not check bitvectors. ShinkaEvolve, LEVI and DGM evolve programs with scalar fitness. Lexicase selection comes from GP without LLMs. Check-vector niches plus lexicase parents plus state-replay return have not been run on a 3-4B tool agent against a 0/64 baseline.
candidates.k2_test:
ARCH-1 (untested; new PREREG before running). Shared K2-3.7B HARD screen: --half subset (210 tasks), thinking off, temp 0.7 / top_p 0.95, 8 plain tries, then 56 more on 0/8 tasks, so HARD = 0/64. PREREQUISITE: the Reach-1 code is not in the /home/user/learner checkout, so first confirm in the sandbox repo that checks come back as a per-check list with names or docstrings that leak no more than Ben-feedback would. A check that reads only the final reply is dropped from the descriptor but kept in the success gate. Use the first 24 HARD tasks; fewer than 12 = inconclusive by design.
ARMS (32 episodes per task; tokens capped at the X-ARCH total ±10%): R+ (32 tries seeing 2 failed transcripts). R+C (32 tries seeing 2 failed transcripts plus their per-check pass/fail lists; the fair control for check information, and the decisive comparison). X-ARCH (8 seed + 3 generations × 8). Lesion arm (report-only): X-RAND, the same archive with uniform random parents and cross pairs.
PASS (fixed): P1 X-ARCH cracks ≥5 HARD. P2 X-ARCH − R+C ≥ 3 tasks, and only-X ≥ 2× only-R+C (paired, McNemar reported). P3 each crack replays ≥2/3 when its final child prompt is re-run 3 times with the replayed prefix. Secondary: archive cells grow each generation, and best-checks-passed rises per generation on ≥60% of tasks.
PROVED WRONG: X-ARCH ≤ R+C, or X-ARCH ≤ 1 crack. Also wrong if ≥ half the cracks are RETURN children of all-but-one parents on tasks R+C also cracks, which would mean the archive only re-finds near misses. A gap of 1-2 is inconclusive: run seed 2 under the same rule. Keep it separate from puzzle/village reporting.
candidates.mac_fit: Serve time adds no model: a JSON archive and a millisecond sandbox replay of a tool prefix. Live on the 8 GB M2: load the archive, make 4-8 children of about 300 tokens with K2 q4 (about 2.6 GB), stop at about 30 s. RETURN children reuse the parent's KV prefix through the warm prompt cache (measured at 0.08 s warm vs 4 s cold). Deep generations run as the Mac's one capped nightly mlx_lm job. RETURN replays only into the sandbox, and real actions still need Ben's confirmation.
candidates.test_cost: Shared screen about 1,680 + about 2,200 confirm episodes (about 2.5-3.5 T4-hours, about half that on the 5070 Ti), reused by the other K2 candidates. Arms: 24 × 32 × 3 ≈ 2,300 episodes, plus about 800 for X-RAND and about 50 replays, roughly 2-3 T4-hours. No API, no Vast. About 150 lines on top of the Reach-1 runner: archive.py, lexicase selection, prefix replay, cross prompt.

closest_work.title: Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (Lu, Hu, Clune)
closest_work.overlap: Closest match for the archive-and-return loop. An LLM judges which states to keep and expand, replacing Go-Explore's hand-written heuristics. Differs from the candidate: cells are states, not check bitvectors. No lexicase, no crossover, no partial-check niches. Its game-of-24 results are the reference point for the Go-Explore half of the idea.

closest_work.title: Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
closest_work.overlap: Archive of coding agents with foundation-model mutation and open-ended parent selection (performance blended with a novelty bonus). Overlaps the archive-plus-LLM-parent loop, and it is a SWE-bench/Polyglot result. Correction to the candidate: DGM is not purely scalar-fitness, since its parent selection already adds a novelty term. Still no per-check vectors, lexicase, or cross-parent recombination of partial wins.

closest_work.title: Evolution through Large Models (ELM, MAP-Elites with LLM mutation)
closest_work.overlap: LLM as the mutation operator inside a MAP-Elites grid over behavior descriptors. Covers the niche-archive part with LLM variation, but the descriptors are hand-chosen behavior features, not per-check pass bits, and there is no lexicase parent choice.

closest_work.title: Digital Red Queen: Adversarial Program Evolution in Core War with LLMs
closest_work.overlap: Reports that ablating MAP-Elites to a single cell hurts optimization, especially late. This is indirect evidence that niching helps LLM program evolution, which supports the candidate's niche assumption. Not a tool-agent or lexicase method.

closest_work.title: Lexicase selection papers (specialists, informed down-sampling, DALex, fast lexicase)
closest_work.overlap: The lexicase parent-selection mechanism over per-case errors, with evidence that it keeps specialists and diversity. All are GP or evolutionary work with no LLM. The candidate's lexicase step is a direct port of this, so the novelty claim rests only on applying it to check-vector archives with LLM agents.

prior.notes: Known-ids check (grep -c on /mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt, 1082 lines): 2603.21357 (AgentHER), 2402.11651 (Wang et al., negative trajectories), 2601.15625 (Fission-GRPO) are already listed. Searches run: 7 web searches, 0 page fetches. Not searched: ShinkaEvolve, LEVI, and the GitHub code side. Searches for LLM plus lexicase (2024-2026) and Go-Explore plus LLM returned no paper combining lexicase over LLM agent outcomes. The candidate's claim that no paper does check-bitvector niches plus lexicase plus state-replay return plus cross-parent recombination was not contradicted, but it was not positively confirmed either (the search engine is weak on these terms). Recommended before the PREREG: (1) read 2509.24116 fully; (2) search GitHub for 'lexicase LLM' and 'go-explore LLM agent' repos; (3) check the candidate's 'why_new' sentence that DGM, LEVI and ShinkaEvolve are scalar-fitness, since DGM is not. Closest prior art that must be cited in any write-up: Intelligent Go-Explore, DGM, ELM/MAP-Elites, lexicase (DALex, fast lexicase). The defensible novelty is the combination (lexicase over per-check bits, plus replay-based return, plus cross of complementary partial wins, on tool agents) rather than any single part."

fatal_flaws: None proven fatal, but one assumption could sink the whole idea and has not been checked (untested): that HARD tasks (0/64) actually give varied partial check vectors. If K2's 64 failed tries on a HARD task mostly pass 0 checks, or all pass the same easy checks (for example 'file exists' but never 'contents right'), the archive has one or two cells. Lexicase then has nothing to choose between, CROSS has no complementary pairs, and the method becomes R+ with extra steps. This can be measured for free from the existing screen logs and must be measured before any new episodes are run.

RETURN needs two things the candidate assumes without evidence (untested). (a) End-state checks must be evaluable on intermediate sandbox states, otherwise 'the step where its last newly-passing check became true' is undefined. (b) Tool replay must be deterministic, with no time, randomness or order-dependent IDs. The Reach-1 code is not in /home/user/learner (I confirmed it is not in the checkout; only unrelated sol_*/premonition scripts match 'checks'). Both are therefore unverified. If either fails, RETURN collapses to 'continue from the end state', which is a different and weaker operator.
fixable_flaws: The baseline is missing the simplest competitor. R+C controls for check information but not for return-and-continue. Add GREEDY-RETURN: always continue from the single try with the most checks passed (fewest turns as tiebreak), with the failing checks named, for 32 episodes, with no archive, no lexicase and no CROSS. If X-ARCH does not beat this arm, the novelty (lexicase plus niches plus crossover) adds nothing beyond plain Go-Explore-style continuation. This should be the decisive comparison, not R+C.

Token matching is underspecified. RETURN children carry a replayed prefix, and CROSS prompts carry two whole transcripts plus pass/fail lists, so prompt tokens can be 3-5x those of R+. Match on prompt plus generated tokens, counting cached prefix tokens at full prompt cost (the cache is a Mac-latency benefit, not a compute advantage on the T4). Also report wall-clock on the Mac.

X-RAND is report-only, so the lexicase claim cannot be falsified. Either promote it to a pre-registered secondary (lexicase X-ARCH minus X-RAND ≥ 2 cracks) or drop 'lexicase protects specialists' from the claims.

Small-model CROSS is risky (suggested). A 3.7B model asked to merge two long tool transcripts is likely to copy one parent. Log, for each CROSS child, whether its check vector is a superset of both parents' passes, and pre-register 'CROSS adds value' as the share of CROSS children that pass a check neither parent passed, or that pass the union, beating the RETURN children's rate.

The Mac live budget is optimistic (suggested). 4-8 children × about 300 generated tokens is 1,200-2,400 tokens. At realistic q4 3.7B speeds on an 8 GB M2 (about 20-35 tok/s) that is 35-120 s, not 30 s, before prompt processing of the transcripts that CROSS includes. Measure it, or set live mode to 2-4 RETURN-only children.

Transfer into first-try behaviour is unaddressed. The puzzle results already show that search finds fits first-try never reproduces (greedy-decoding bottleneck). P3 checks that a crack replays with the same prompt and prefix, not that a card or LoRA makes the plain first try succeed. Add P4 (report-only): after one morning card/LoRA step, plain 8-try pass rate on the cracked tasks versus R+C cracks given the same treatment.

The real-use analog is thin (suggested). Ben's real tasks rarely recur exactly, so a per-task archive that persists across nights mostly helps nightly stuck-low tasks, not new ones. Feedback like 'that part is right but X is wrong' gives about 1-2 bits, not a 5-check vector. Real actions such as mail or calendar are not deterministically replayable, so RETURN is sandbox-only, as the candidate already admits. State this plainly instead of claiming a live analog.

Correct the why_new line. DGM selects parents with a novelty term, not pure scalar fitness, and ShinkaEvolve and LEVI were not checked. The defensible novelty is the combination: lexicase over per-check bits, exact replay return, and complementary crossover, on a small tool agent. Also cite Intelligent Go-Explore as the nearest work.

Small numbers. With 24 tasks and expected cracks in the single digits, McNemar has almost no power. Keep the fixed absolute thresholds as the decision rule, keep McNemar descriptive, and pre-commit to seed 2 on a 1-2 gap, as the candidate already does.
attack.fair_baseline: Same 24 HARD tasks, paired, with an equal budget of prompt plus generated tokens (cached prefix counted at full cost), ±10%. (1) R+C: 32 tries, each seeing 2 failed transcripts plus their per-check pass/fail lists. This controls for check information. (2) GREEDY-RETURN: 8 plain seeds, then 24 continuations, each from the current max-checks try's exact replayed state with the failing checks named, updating the 'best' try as it improves. This controls for return-and-continue without archive, lexicase or crossover. The decisive comparison is X-ARCH against the better of these two arms on each task.
attack.likely_effect: Untested overall. Suggested: some lift over R+C is plausible on HARD tasks where gen-0 tries pass different checks. That lift will mostly come from RETURN (continuing from a real partial state with the failing checks named), and GREEDY-RETURN will probably capture most of it. Lexicase and CROSS are likely to add little on a 3.7B model with tasks that have about 3-6 checks, because lexicase needs many cases to matter and small models merge transcripts poorly. Shown: nothing yet. The relevant shown results are negative for adjacent ideas (hindsight relabel and composition failed on the puzzle model; search finds fits first-try does not reproduce), and they argue against expecting the gain to carry over into weights. Expected size if it works: +1 to +4 cracks out of 24 against R+C, and 0 to +2 against GREEDY-RETURN.
attack.improved_test:
ARCH-1, rewritten. Keep it separate from puzzle and village reporting, and write a new PREREG first.

STAGE 0 (free, no new episodes; run first on the existing K2 HARD screen logs once the Reach-1 repo is located):
- Confirm that checks return per-check results.
- Confirm that checks can be evaluated on intermediate states.
- Confirm that a replayed tool prefix reproduces the same sandbox state on 20/20 sampled prefixes.
- For each HARD task, using its 64 failed tries, compute:
  (a) the number of distinct non-zero check vectors;
  (b) the union of checks passed across all 64 tries (does it cover every check?);
  (c) whether any pair of tries is complementary.
- GO only if ≥50% of HARD tasks have ≥3 distinct non-zero vectors and ≥30% have union coverage of all checks. Otherwise DROP: there are no stepping stones to keep. Report the average number of checks per task. If the median is ≤3, drop lexicase from the claims, since it cannot differ from best-first.

STAGE 1 (only if Stage 0 says GO): first 24 HARD tasks; fewer than 12 qualifying tasks = inconclusive. Arms, paired on the same tasks with equal prompt plus generated tokens ±10% (cached prefix counted at full cost):
- R+C: 32 tries seeing 2 failed transcripts plus check lists.
- GREEDY-RETURN: 8 seeds, then 24 continuations from the current best partial try's replayed state.
- X-ARCH: 8 seeds + 3 generations × 8, half RETURN and half CROSS.
- X-RAND: X-ARCH with uniform random parents.

Fixed pass marks:
- P1: X-ARCH cracks ≥5 tasks.
- P2 (decisive): X-ARCH minus max(R+C, GREEDY-RETURN) ≥3 tasks, and only-X-ARCH cracks ≥2× only-other cracks.
- P3: each crack reproduces ≥2/3 on re-run.
- P4 (pre-registered secondary): X-ARCH minus X-RAND ≥2 tasks. If not met, drop the lexicase claim.
- P5: CROSS children reach a passed-check union, or pass a check neither parent passed, at a higher rate than RETURN children. If not met, drop CROSS.

Proved wrong if any of these hold:
- X-ARCH ≤ GREEDY-RETURN;
- X-ARCH cracks ≤1 task;
- ≥ half the cracks are RETURN children of an all-but-one parent on tasks GREEDY-RETURN also cracks.

A gap of 1-2 tasks: run seed 2 under the same rule.

Mac check, in the same PREREG: measure live wall-clock for 4 RETURN children on the 8 GB M2 and on the M1 Pro. The live mode is viable only at ≤45 s median.

Transfer, report-only: after one morning card step, the plain 8-try pass rate on X-ARCH cracks versus R+C cracks.

Cost: Stage 0 is about 0 GPU-hours. Stage 1 is about 24 × 32 × 4 ≈ 3,100 episodes, roughly 3-4 T4-hours, or about half that on the 5070 Ti after 14:00Z on Oct 26 (the second Kaggle account is also an option). No API, no Vast.

candidates.name: Verified Ladder: build checkable easier siblings of the stuck job in its own world, climb them, then sleep on them
candidates.one_line: When a task is stuck, make a small tree of nearby easier jobs that still have real checks. Some are made by code (drop a check, shrink the world, keep only the first sub-goal), others by the model (same goal on another item, undo it, a read-only probe, each with a harness-run self-check). Keep only siblings the model solves sometimes but not always, show the solved ones to the real job as same-world stepping stones, learn which kinds of change pay off, and at night train on the verified sibling wins so the ladder moves back toward the original and greedy first-try improves.
candidates.mechanism:
STORED: a ladder tree per stuck task. Each node holds the variant task, its check set or edited world, the operator used, its distance from the original in steps, its solve rate at 8 tries, and its best solving transcript. Plus a Beta-Bernoulli credit table over (operator × failure signature), where the failure signature is one of 5 rule-based classes read from the failed transcripts: repeated tool error / asked when it should act / acted when it should ask / wrong entity / stopped early.
OPERATORS. Code-only, so the checker is always real: RELAX (drop one end-state check from the gate), SHRINK (remove distractor files, records or tools from the world; the same checks apply), SPLIT (keep only the checks for the first named sub-goal). Model-written, each with a self-check made of read-only tool calls with expected values that the harness runs; the model never grades itself in words: SWAP (same goal on another entity in this world), INVERT (undo or reach the opposite state), PROBE (answer a read-only question the job depends on), DISAMBIGUATE (one clarifying sentence chosen from what the failed tries got wrong).
STAGE A, DAY OR NIGHT SEARCH: (1) Operators are chosen by Thompson sampling from the credit table, and K=4-6 children are made. (2) MINIMAL CRITERION: run 8 tries per child and keep it only if 1-6 of 8 pass (learnable, not trivial). Prune duplicates by solving tool-sequence. (3) CLIMB: T gets 8 tries with the R+ block plus up to 2 solved sibling transcripts, labelled 'A smaller version of this job, solved in this same world'. The tool results come from T's own world, which fixes BORROW's cross-world copying. (4) DOWNSTREAM CREDIT: an operator earns 1 only if T is cracked in a try that saw its stone. Solving the sibling itself earns nothing.
STAGE B, NIGHT WEIGHTS: a rank-16 LoRA with the existing KL anchor, trained on solved-sibling trajectories (each on its own variant request, never relabelled) plus climb wins plus a replay mix of normal-task wins. The next night mutates from the new frontier, one step closer to the original. Optional: DPO for the morph-writer, with chosen = a morph whose stone led to a crack and rejected = a morph that was solved but did not help (useful vs merely easy reframing).
REAL USE: for a stuck real task, the assistant builds a shrunken sandbox copy of the folder overnight, one sub-goal at a time. The verified path ('first do A, then the rest') becomes a playbook card. One model throughout; the mutators are code.
candidates.why_fantastic: On a 0/64 task every training signal is zero by definition, which is why single-try RL, hindsight and dream school had nothing to grab. This makes real positive examples one checked step away from the exact failure, keeps them only where they carry signal (minimal criterion), and lets the frontier move each night, so the task set and the model evolve together (POET / minimal-criterion coevolution). It is Polya's 'solve a related easier problem' as a checkable, learned loop, with a credit table that learns which changes of the problem pay off for which kind of stuckness. 'More sleep nights' is the only thing that reliably helped on the puzzle model, and this aims those nights at the frontier instead of at random dreams. It also attacks the greedy bottleneck: wins found by search go into the weights, and the test measures greedy first-try on the original.
candidates.why_new: Random dream school made puzzles far from any failure, while this makes checker-safe one-step variants of the specific stuck task. Hindsight/AgentHER/ECHO change the goal after the fact, while here the variant's goal is fixed before the try and checked. FLIP changes the approach, while this changes the task. BORROW copies another world's solution. Incubation (queued) retries the same task. LADDER (2503.00735) does easier integral variants with a numeric verifier and test-time RL; this adds a tool sandbox, same-world stones, code-only check-relax and world-shrink operators, minimal-criterion filtering, downstream-credit operator learning and frontier-tracking sleep. Absolute Zero and R-Zero invent problems with no anchor to a deployed failure.
candidates.k2_test:
LADDER-1, two pre-registered stages run in order (one change at a time). Shared K2 HARD screen. PREREQUISITE: confirm that the task JSON exposes a check list and world items that code can drop. If RELAX, SHRINK and SPLIT are impossible, the code half is void; do not fall back to model-written checks for the gate. Also confirm whether any check reads the reply text; if so, self-checks are tool-call-only and real-check results are reported split into world and reply checks.
STAGE A (search; split HARD by scenario: train for the credit table, test scored). ARMS on HARD-test, all generated tokens counted, including morph calls and sibling tries: R+ (extra tries up to the ML token total, cap 28). ML (4-6 siblings, MC filter, climb, uniform operators). ML-noSol (the same sibling requests shown as 'smaller versions to think about', with no solved transcripts and the same budget). ML-T (Thompson prior learned on HARD-train and the 1-4/64 tasks). PASS: ML cracks ≥5; ML − R+ ≥ 3 with only-ML ≥ 2× only-R+; ML − ML-noSol ≥ 2; wins replay ≥2/3 with the same stones. Report-only: ML-T − ML. PROVED WRONG: ML ≤ R+ (tokens-matched), or ML ≤ ML-noSol (the wording helps, the climbing does not). AUDIT: the share of stones that pass their own self-check but break a real check when run on T's checks.
STAGE B (only if A passes or is inconclusive; weights): split HARD 50/50 into LADDER-TRAIN and HELD-OUT, plus the 100 normal held-out tasks. 3 nights per arm, same LoRA recipe and replay mix, 52 episodes per LADDER-TRAIN task per night. Baseline STaR+R+: the same 52 episodes as R+ tries on the originals, then sleep on any wins plus the same replay. Eval after night 3, greedy and pass@8. PASS: greedy cracks ≥4 LADDER-TRAIN originals and ≥ baseline +3; HELD-OUT pass@8 ≥ baseline +3; normal held-out drop ≤3 points. PROVED WRONG: LADDER ≤ baseline on both, or the gain shows only with climb context and not in greedy without context. Gaps of 1-2 are inconclusive and go to seed 2.
candidates.mac_fit: Serve time adds nothing new: K2 q4 plus a 30-60 MB nightly LoRA in mlx_lm on the 8 GB M2 or M1 Pro. The ladder tree is small JSON plus shrunken world copies on disk. Live use is capped at 2 siblings × 1 try + 4 target tries within 30 s, with the full ladder deferred to night. A night for 5-10 real stuck tasks is about 1-2 h of K2 q4 generation plus the existing sleep step (cap 3 tasks on the 8 GB tier). Sandbox-only: variants are copies.
candidates.test_cost: Stage A: about 2,400 episodes on top of the shared screen, about 1-1.5 h on the 5070 Ti or 3 on a T4. Stage B: about 4,700 episodes plus 6 LoRA runs (about 1.5 h) plus about 2,300 eval episodes, about 6.5-8 T4-hours or about 4 on the 5070 Ti. The runner must be resumable across Kaggle sessions. No API.
