prior.notes: Verdict: partly-new. The reverse-retrieval core (a new win is pushed against a board of stored open failures, indexed by a blocked-at signature) did not appear in the 7 searches I ran (budget was 8), and the 4 page fetches were not used. The parts that are not new: (a) contrastive win-vs-fail insight extraction (ExpeL 2308.10144, already in known-ids; ReasoningBank 2509.25140, also known); (b) step-level pairs at the divergence point (ETO 2403.02502 known; 2606.23112, IPR 2406.11176, LACL-GUI 2608.21830, CSO 2602.03412 not known); (c) cross-task failure-to-lesson memory (2026 papers above). The candidate's why_new says 'playbook cards are built from wins with no contrast against failures.' ExpeL and ReasoningBank both contrast wins and failures, so that sentence needs narrowing before it is cited. The candidate also names Blocks, DreamCoder, LATM, TroVE, PivoARL, Reflective Recovery and ECHO as the nearest neighbours. I did not verify those, so the 'none keeps a cross-task board' claim is unchecked. Known-ids checks: 2308.10144, 2403.02502, 2409.07429 (AWM), 2303.11366 (Reflexion), 2305.16291 (Voyager), 2509.25140, 2502.12110 are present. 2406.11176, 2608.21830, 2610.25790, 2610.22984, 2606.31270, 2607.28156, 2610.08048, 2603.10600, 2602.03412 and 2606.23112 are not in known-ids, and the grep was not run on 2606.23112 or 2602.03412 (the two IDs were taken from search results, so treat them as unverified until grepped). Two ids in the search output are not arXiv ids and were not verified: the Lacuna 'first-failure step preferences' note and the psychology incubation chapter. Recommended next check: a search for 'open problem board' or 'lifelong retry queue' in agents, and a fetch of 2606.23112 to see whether its divergence-point DPO is run across tasks or within one task. The single-task vs cross-task distinction is the part that could still make the candidate new.

fatal_flaws: PREP-1 does not test the part that is new. At retry time, arm K is forward retrieval: take the live failure, look up short contrastive rules by a structural key, and put them in the prompt. That is ExpeL/ReasoningBank with Jaccard over blocked-at features in place of embeddings. The new claim, 'a win goes looking for old failures', only shows up in Stage 2, and Stage 2 is compared against plain R+ rather than against forward retrieval from the same growing library. As designed, a PREP-1 PASS cannot show that the reverse direction adds anything. (shown, from the design text)

The Stage 2 baseline is unfair. 'Board gets 4 extra R+ tries per night' leaves out the obvious rival: a periodic retry of each open row with forward-retrieved moves from the same library, at the same number of tries. Without that arm, Prepared Mind is the same as 'ExpeL plus a retry queue'. The only difference is scheduling: retries triggered by a new move arriving versus retries on a timer. (shown)
fixable_flaws: The KR random-move control is too weak. Random moves include junk extracted from noisy diffs, so K > KR could just mean 'good generic rules beat bad ones'. Add KP: the top-8 most popular or most reliable moves, with no matching. Matching only counts if K beats KP. (suggested)

The diff extraction is fragile at 8 tries. With 1 pass and 7 fails, the '>=80% of passes' test is met by any step in that single pass, so spurious diffs will dominate. Require >=2 passes and >=2 fails, and say whether 'contains the step' means at aligned index k or anywhere as a tool bigram. Normalised position alignment breaks when passes take different-length routes. (suggested)

There is no check that extraction works at all. Inject each move back into its own source task and its siblings (with the source's own transcripts excluded). If the moves do not lift their own source tasks, the K arm is testing broken rules. (untested, cheap)

The signature feature space is coarse: about 5 error classes, the last tool, a step index and the never-called tools. Many HARD failures may share one signature, for example 'no tool call' or 'empty result'. Matching then collapses to 'same top-2 moves for everyone', which is really KP. Pre-register a check on signature entropy and ties. (untested)

Possible template leakage: mixed tasks and HARD tasks come from the same 420-task sandbox, and sibling templates may share a solution. Report results split by task family. Count a crack as cross-family only when the source and target families differ. (untested)

Power is low. The pass mark of 'K - R+ >= 3' over roughly 8-30 HARD tasks is within noise for near-zero base rates. Fix a paired exact test (sign test on discordant tasks) and a seed-2 rule in advance. (suggested)
KT should not be report-only. Decisive move versus whole transcript is one of the two claims in 'why_fantastic', so give it a pass mark. (suggested)

why_new says playbook cards and prior work have 'no contrast against failures'. That is false: ExpeL and ReasoningBank both contrast wins and failures. The 'none keeps a cross-task board' claim is also unchecked. Step-level DPO at the divergence point is prior art (ETO, IPR, 2606.23112, CSO). (shown by the prior-art check)

The test does not reuse existing work. Reach-1 is paused at 270 episodes with an R+ arm already defined on HARD = 0/64 tasks. If the code, prompts and seeds match, reuse that R+ data and that HARD set as the control instead of building a new 0/32 screen. Decide what happens to Reach-1 first, so two creative-mode tests do not split the 5070 Ti. (suggested)

Puzzle-model history counts against prompt-level hints: hindsight relabel, composition and aha picking all failed, and the stated bottleneck is greedy decoding. The day mode only adds about 60 prompt tokens, and nothing shows that a hint changes the greedy first try. Add a greedy, first-try-only measure to the K and R+ arms. (untested)
attack.fair_baseline: Equal tries and matched extra-block length on the same HARD tasks. (a) R+ (retries that see failed tries). (b) KP: R+ plus the 8 most popular or most reliable library moves, with no matching. (c) For Stage 2: forward retrieval, where each open board row is retried on a fixed schedule with its top matched moves pulled at retry time from the same growing library, at the same tries per night as the event-triggered reverse match. Only (c) can separate 'a solution looks for a problem' from 'ExpeL plus a retry queue'.
attack.likely_effect: Mac fit is good. This is shown from the design: serving is prompt text plus Python Jaccard, about 60 tokens, with K2 q4 unchanged. A small lift over R+ on HARD tasks is suggested. Generic short procedural rules such as 'list_dir before edit' plausibly crack a few tool-sandbox stalls, but most of that lift is likely to come from good generic rules (KP) rather than from signature matching. Whether matching beats popularity is untested. Whether the reverse direction beats forward retrieval is untested, and the current design does not test it. Whether hints change greedy first tries (the known bottleneck) is untested. That step-level DPO will help is suggested by prior art (ETO, IPR) but untested here. Real-use benefit is suggested at best: Ben's real requests seldom produce 8 tries with mixed outcomes, and many real stuck tasks cannot be replayed in a sandbox to close a board row.
attack.improved_test: PREP-1' (tool sandbox only, new PREREG; Reach-1's prereg is not edited). Stage 0, no GPU: run the blocked-at signature code on existing Reach-1 HARD failure logs. Stop if one signature covers more than 40% of HARD rows, because matching would be degenerate. Stage 1, sanity: extract moves only from mixed tasks with >=2 passes and >=2 fails. Inject each move into its own source family's other tasks (with the source's own transcripts excluded), 8 tries with and without the move. Moves must lift their own family by >=15 points on average, or extraction is broken: stop. Stage 2, arms on HARD tasks (reuse the Reach-1 HARD set and its R+ data if the code is identical; otherwise 0/32, with N >= 12 required), 16 tries each, extra block matched within 10%: R+; K (matched moves); KP (top-8 popular moves, unmatched); KR (random moves); KT (whole source transcripts). Also log a greedy single try with the top-2 matched moves against greedy with none. PASS, fixed in advance: K cracks >=4 tasks; K beats R+ by >=3 tasks with a one-sided sign test on discordant tasks, p<0.1; K beats KP by >=2 tasks (this is the matching claim); K >= KT; >=50% of K cracks cross-family; each crack replays >=2/3. PROVED WRONG: K <= KP (matching adds nothing beyond good generic rules) or K <= R+. Between those: seed 2 once. Stage 3, the drain test, only if PASS: stream 4 days of 80 tasks. Pass: (i) closes >=1.5x the rows of (ii) by day 4. Otherwise the novel part is dropped and the idea collapses into ExpeL-style playbook cards, which is still worth keeping as cards. candidates.name: Night Lab: overnight read-only experiments that turn failures into verified facts about the tools
candidates.one_line: At night the creative mode does not retry a stuck task. It runs a scientist's loop: list what about the tools or world might differ from what the attempts assumed, design one tiny discriminating probe per guess in a throwaway sandbox copy, and keep the raw observed outputs as a growing, cross-task library of verified tool facts. Later tries get facts, not advice, and recurring facts go into the weights as a world model of its own tools.
candidates.mechanism:
STORED: a fact library, one row per fact: (tool, normalised argument shape, situation) → observed output quoted verbatim from a real sandbox call, plus a one-line model gloss marked UNVERIFIED and a count of tasks it was relevant to. Examples: 'search_orders(name="Smith") returns [] but name="smith" returns 2 rows'; 'edit_file on a missing path silently creates a file and reports ok'.
NIGHT, per stuck task: (1) HYPOTHESES: one K2 call on the 2 failed transcripts: 'List up to 4 things about the tools or world that, if different from what the attempts assumed, would explain the failure, each with ONE short tool call that would tell which is true.' Unlike FLIP, which reverses an assumption and acts on it untested, each guess must carry a discriminating experiment. (2) PROBES: each runs in a fresh copy of the task's world, 1-3 turns, and never runs the task's checks (so it cannot game them). The world is thrown away afterwards. (3) RECORD: keep (call, raw output). The model may label it 'confirms/refutes H2', but only the raw output counts as verified. Duplicates are merged across tasks by (tool, argument shape); facts seen on ≥3 tasks are promoted.
DAY: when creative mode fires, attach the facts for the tools named in the request and the failed transcript, at most 6 facts and about 200 tokens ('Facts observed in this environment: ...').
WEIGHTS (later, recurring only): promoted facts become short SFT question-answer pairs ('What does search_orders return for a lowercase name?' → the observed output) in the nightly KL-anchored LoRA, so the first greedy try is right without the sheet.
REAL USE: on Ben's Mac, probes are limited to read-only calls (ls, stat, search, list), which matches the existing rule for live creative actions.
candidates.why_fantastic: Every planned operator and paper on the map changes what the model SAYS next. None changes what it KNOWS about its world, and many hard tool failures are knowledge failures: a wrong belief about a tool's behaviour that every sample shares, so resampling cannot fix it. Night Lab makes incubation an active experiment whose overnight insight is a measured fact. It cannot be a hallucinated 'aha' (the aha/MDL failure) and cannot game the checks. Facts are about shared tools, so one night's probes on task A help tasks B to Z. For Ben's real Mac work it becomes an ever-growing, verified manual of how his own environment actually behaves, learned by the assistant itself.
candidates.why_new: FLIP reverses assumptions without testing them. Incubation (brain test 3) retries with failed guesses banned. Playbook cards, AWM, Synapse, ReasoningBank and ACE store procedures or strategies. LATM, TroVE and trick 4 build tools. ECHO and AgentHER relabel goals. Absolute Zero and R-Zero make new tasks, not experiments about an existing failure. LaMer explores inside the episode for reward. None separates an unscored hypothesis-and-probe phase from the solve phase, stores only raw observed tool behaviour, and shares it across tasks by tool signature. Tool-fact SFT teaches environment semantics, not trajectories.
candidates.k2_test:
LAB-1 (tool sandbox only). The same K2 HARD set and screen as PREP-1 (0/32 on --half, MIN_HARD 8), with HARD split by id parity into halves A and B. Prerequisite: a 'fresh world copy, no checks' runner mode for probes (a small runner change, not a PREREG edit).
ARMS, matched on total generated + prompt tokens (measure the probe cost, then top up R+): R+ (about 16 tries). L (the lab on this task, then 12 solve tries with the R+ block + its own facts). LS (12 tries with the R+ block + facts from a DIFFERENT HARD task's lab, same length and format: any fact sheet or extra length). LX (half B only: no own probes, 16 tries with facts from half A's library chosen by tool-name match: the library claim).
PASS (fixed): L cracks ≥4; L − R+ ≥ 3 with only-L ≥ 2× only-R+ (paired); L − LS ≥ 2; wins replay ≥2/3 with the same sheet. Secondary but pre-registered: LX − R+ ≥ 2 on half B.
PROVED WRONG: L ≤ R+ at matched tokens, or L ≤ LS (the facts are not what helps). If L passes and LX fails, the cross-task library claim is wrong ('helps only the probed task'). Diagnostic: the share of L wins whose transcript uses a tool or argument pattern named in a probed fact; under 50% suggests the win came from extra context. The weights stage is out of scope (one change at a time).
candidates.mac_fit: Serve time: a sheet of at most 200 tokens chosen by tool-name lookup, with K2 q4 unchanged, so it fits the 8 GB M2. The night lab is about 6-8k tokens per stuck task, so 20 tasks is under 200k tokens in the Mac's capped mlx job. Probes run only in throwaway sandbox copies, and live probes are read-only.
candidates.test_cost: About 1 GPU-hour on top of the shared screen (lab about 100 short episodes, arms about 960 episodes plus replays), about 2.5 GPU-hours standalone on the 5070 Ti (5-6 on a Kaggle T4). No API, $0. Cheapest candidate, so a good first run while the PC is busy.

closest_work.title: WebATLAS: An LLM Agent with Experience-Driven Memory and Action Simulation
closest_work.overlap: Curiosity-driven exploration of the environment before evaluation, with no task reward, seeds memory with LLM-written summaries of transitions and site rules. Closest match to 'explore overnight, carry facts into later tasks'. Differs: summaries are model-written, not raw verified outputs; no per-guess discriminating probe; no tool-signature library.

closest_work.title: AutoManual: Constructing Instruction Manuals by LLM Agents via Interactive Environmental Learning
closest_work.overlap: Agents learn an environment by interaction and build a reusable rule manual; has a Testing stage. Differs: stores LLM-generated generalized rules, not raw observed tool outputs; no hypothesis-then-probe design; not shared by tool signature across tasks.

closest_work.title: LLMs in the Imaginarium: Tool Learning through Simulated Trial and Error
closest_work.overlap: Exploration phase probes each new API under a call budget, reflects on responses, then exploits the gathered experience. Closest on 'probe tools to learn their behaviour'. Differs: no separate unscored hypothesis stage, no sandbox-copy isolation as described, no promoted cross-task fact library (per snippet).

closest_work.title: The Little Scientist: LLM Agent-Driven Discovery via the Scientific Method
closest_work.overlap: Scientific-method loop: hypotheses, experiments, failed hypotheses narrow later proposals, predictions reconciled with feedback. Overlaps the hypothesis-probe-record loop. Differs: aimed at discovery in a system, not a store of verified tool facts for solve-time retrieval (not read in full).

closest_work.title: HExA (Interphyre benchmark)
closest_work.overlap: Actor and evolver design experiments, test hypotheses, distill reusable skills. Overlaps the experiment-then-store part. Differs: distils procedural skills, not raw tool-output facts (snippet only).

closest_work.title: Teaching LLMs to Learn Tool Trialing and Execution through Environment Interaction (ToolMaster)
closest_work.overlap: Model calls tools to see responses before planning, then trains via SFT and RL. Overlaps the 'tool behaviour learned into the weights' stage. Differs: trains on trajectories from a teacher, not on short QA pairs of verified tool facts.

closest_work.title: Agent2World: Learning to Generate Symbolic World Models via Adaptive Multi-Agent Feedback
closest_work.overlap: Builds world models from execution feedback and fine-tunes on them. Overlaps 'learned world model of the environment'. Differs: symbolic models of the environment, not a fact library with probing and promotion.

closest_work.title: Learning Hierarchical Procedural Memory for LLM Agents (MACLA)
closest_work.overlap: Procedures learned from trajectories and verified in the environment, with exploration/consolidation phases. Overlaps 'verified memory across tasks'. Differs: stores procedures, not tool-behaviour facts.

prior.notes: Verdict: partly-new. Each component has precedent (exploration before tasks: WebATLAS, AutoManual, Imaginarium; hypothesis-driven experiments: Little Scientist, HExA; learning tool behaviour into weights: ToolMaster, Agent2World). I did not find a paper that combines all of: discriminating probe per guess, isolated sandbox copy with no checks, raw-output-only storage keyed by tool signature, count-based promotion across tasks, and SFT of promoted facts. Confidence is limited: 7 web searches, 0 page fetches, so every row above rests on search snippets. Known-ids check: none of the IDs I tried (2609.11060, 2602.23008, 2512.18950, 2510.22732, 2405.16247, 2601.09503, 2403.04746, 2608.16951, 2606.29315, 2610.11253, 2601.12762, 2512.22336, 2609.34151, 2605.18421) appears in /mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt (1082 lines), so that list does not cover this area; a 'not in list' result is not evidence of novelty. Not checked in this pass: the candidate's cited prior art (FLIP, AWM, Synapse, ReasoningBank, ACE, ECHO, AgentHER, Absolute Zero, R-Zero, LaMer, TroVE, LATM, incubation). The candidate's why_new depends on those and should be verified before the novelty claim is relied on. Most exposed claim: that no prior work stores tool facts as raw observed outputs for cross-task reuse; WebATLAS and AutoManual are the papers to read in full first. Suggested check: fetch arXiv 2510.22732 and 2405.16247 and confirm whether they store raw observations or only model-written summaries."

fatal_flaws: Untested and likely the deciding issue: the plan assumes HARD failures are mostly knowledge failures, meaning a wrong belief about how a tool behaves that every sample shares. I only spot-checked 10 rows of /mnt/project-files/rlaif/kaggle-run1/runs/eval_base/eval_base.jsonl, so this is suggested, not shown. Those rows show scenario types like clarify, confirm_irreversible, multi_step, parallel and summarize_long. They also show answers that claim the job is done after only 2 turns (h002 says it 'appended the code and set a reminder' in 2 turns and failed both checks). Failures like these come from policy, diligence or hallucinated completion. They are not wrong beliefs about tools, so no probe can reveal a fact that fixes them. If fewer than about a quarter of the HARD tasks have a fact that can be probed, L cannot reach the pass marks no matter how well it is built. This should be measured before any GPU time is spent.

The baseline is missing an obvious arm (shown by the design itself). L's probes run in a fresh copy of the same task's world, so the 'lab' is really a scouting pass of that task: it can, for example, ls the directory and find the file that error_recovery says is missing. The fair rival is not only R+. It is R+ tries told to spend their first turns on read-only probes inside the episode, at matched tokens (R+P). Without R+P, a win for L cannot be told apart from 'explore before acting', which is old (ReAct-style scouting, the STE exploration phase). As written, the novelty and gain claims cannot be told apart.
fixable_flaws: Too few tasks (suggested). With MIN_HARD 8 split by id parity, each half holds about 4 to 8 tasks. A pre-registered LX − R+ ≥ 2 on half B is roughly coin-flip noise. Either pool more HARD tasks (relax the screen to 0/32 on the full set, or add the 'stuck low' tasks), or demote LX to exploratory and say so before the run.

The cross-task library claim is untested and may be empty by construction. Each Reach-1 task builds its own mock world, so most 'facts' (file paths, note contents) are task-local. Before the run, count how many HARD tasks share a tool whose real behaviour differs from its schema docstring. Fewer than about 3 shared quirky tools means the library has nothing to share.

Facts may just restate the tool schema (suggested). The tools are probably clean mocks whose behaviour matches their descriptions. Add a 'schema-only sheet' control: the same 200 tokens, restating tool docs. L must beat it, or the 'facts' are just docs read aloud.

Greedy decoding is a known bottleneck. The replay rule (≥2/3 with the same sheet) should include one greedy first try with the sheet, since that is how the system is actually served. Otherwise a sampled win can pass the replay test and still never show up in real use.

The win diagnostic ('transcript uses a tool or argument pattern named in a fact') is too loose, because almost any transcript reuses the same tools. Instead, require the winning transcript to make a call that the fact's verbatim output would change: for example, it uses the lowercase name after the fact showed case sensitivity.
The prior-art check rests on search snippets only (0 page fetches). Read AutoManual, WebATLAS and the Imaginarium STE paper in full before claiming that raw-output-only storage is new.
A 'fresh world copy, no checks' runner mode is needed. Confirm it truly resets state, including any shared mock state between calls, so probe side effects cannot carry into the solve tries.
attack.fair_baseline: Run four arms, all at matched total prompt + generated tokens on the same HARD tasks, with the same R+ failure block: (1) R+, about 16 tries that see failed tries. (2) R+P: R+ tries with an instruction to first make up to 3 read-only probe calls and state what they learned, then solve. This is in-episode scouting with the same budget. (3) LS: someone else's facts. (4) a schema-only sheet. L must beat R+P and LS, not just R+.
attack.likely_effect: Suggested: small to none on Reach-1 HARD, because the failure types sampled (clarify, confirm_irreversible, stopping early, hallucinated completion) are not tool-knowledge failures. Any L win over R+ will probably shrink to near zero against R+P, because the own-world probes act as scouting. Untested: the cross-task library effect (LX). It is probably near zero here, because each mock world is task-specific. Suggested: higher value on Ben's real Mac, where the environment is persistent and shared across tasks (paths, venvs, commands that fail, file layouts). There, a verified, read-only, growing manual of his own machine is useful. But it overlaps ordinary memory/notes, and Reach-1 cannot measure that.
attack.improved_test: LAB-0, a ceiling audit with no GPU (about $1 of Batches API, or by hand). For every HARD task, label the 2 failed transcripts: is there a fact about the tools or world, findable with ≤3 read-only calls in a fresh copy, whose truth would have changed the failing action? Record the fact and whether it is task-local (this world's files) or tool-level (shared across tasks). Pass marks fixed now: ≥40% of HARD tasks have a probe-able fact, and ≥3 tool-level facts recur on ≥2 tasks. Proved wrong / drop: <25% probe-able, or zero recurring tool-level facts, which means the library claim is dead on Reach-1. LAB-0b, an oracle ceiling (about 0.3 GPU-hour). Give R+ tries the hand-written TRUE fact (≤200 tokens) on the probe-able tasks. If the oracle sheet gives < +3 cracks over R+ at matched tokens, model-found facts cannot do better: stop. Only if both pass, run LAB-1 with these arms at matched tokens: R+, R+P (in-episode scouting), L, LS, schema-only sheet. Fixed passes: L ≥ 4 cracks; L − R+P ≥ 2 with only-L ≥ 2× only-R+P (paired); L − LS ≥ 2; L − schema ≥ 2; ≥1 of 3 greedy first tries with the sheet succeeds on each counted win. Proved wrong: L ≤ R+P (it is just scouting) or L ≤ LS. Keep LX as exploratory unless the half-B task count is ≥ 10. Separately, and outside the Reach-1 claim, a Mac pilot: log 2 weeks of Ben's real stuck episodes, then count how many hinged on an environment fact that a read-only probe would have revealed. That count, not Reach-1, decides real-use value. Plain-language summary for Ben: the idea is that at night, instead of trying a stuck task again, the assistant runs tiny safe experiments to learn how its tools really behave and writes down exactly what it saw. First we check, almost for free, whether our hard tasks actually fail because the model misunderstands a tool. If they mostly fail for other reasons, such as not asking you first or claiming it finished when it didn't, then fact sheets can't help, and we save the GPU time.

ranking.name: Doubt Forks: force the runner-up at the model's confident decisions, and learn which confidences to doubt
ranking.reason: HEADLINE. It is the only candidate aimed straight at the one bottleneck we have measured: on the puzzle model, search finds answers that greedy first-try never reproduces. Forked one-token-diff DPO pairs put the training signal on the exact token where greedy went wrong. It also does not depend on how many checks a task has. That matters because the only Reach-style logs I could read (/mnt/project-files/rlaif/kaggle-run1/runs/eval_base/eval_base.jsonl, 100 tasks, model not confirmed as K2) have a median of 2 checks per task, 27% of tasks with a single check, and many failures that are early 'done' claims or quitting after an error after only 2 turns. Those are exactly the confident decision points a turn-start fork can flip. The test is cheap: a CPU/Mac gate needing no GPU, then roughly 3.5 GPU-hours on the 5070 Ti for 2 seeds. Novelty is only partial (divergence-point DPO exists in 2606.23112), so the claim rests on forcing the logprob runner-up at confident tokens. The DF-ent and DF-loc controls test that claim directly.

ranking.name: Impasse Forge: break the route that worked, on purpose, so the creative mode practises getting unstuck where a way out is certified
ranking.reason: BACKUP. Most ambitious answer to the zero-signal problem: it manufactures solvable stuck states from our own wins every night, with ground-truth checks and no narration loophole. It fits real use better than most (error_recovery-type quitting shows up in the logs). It depends on the HARD failure mix being 'route-blocked', which a $2 triage measures before any GPU time. It costs more than Doubt Forks and is close to Fission-GRPO, so novelty rests on P3 (beating random-block training).

ranking.name: Check-Lexicase Stepping-Stone Archive (Go-Explore over partial wins)
ranking.reason: The most open-ended idea, and on paper the purest 'new kind of search'. But the readable logs suggest Reach tasks carry 1-2 checks, rarely 3. With 2 checks there are at most 3 non-zero check vectors, and with 1 check there is just 1. Lexicase then reduces to best-first, CROSS has almost no complementary pairs, and the advisor's own Stage-0 gate (>=3 distinct non-zero vectors on >=50% of HARD tasks) will probably fail. The useful part, GREEDY-RETURN (continue from the replayed state of the best partial try), should be kept as a cheap add-on arm later. On this test bed it should not be the headline.

ranking.name: Verified Ladder: build checkable easier siblings of the stuck job in its own world, climb them, then sleep on them
ranking.reason: Sound curriculum logic, and SHRINK is a genuinely new operator. Its code operators also need several droppable checks, though, and RELAX is impossible on single-check tasks. The advisor expects the gain over R+check to be 0-2. Its weight stage is the same composition bet that failed on the puzzle model. Novelty is lowest among the strong ideas (LADDER, ARQ).

ranking.name: Set-Credit Reframer: a learned creative LoRA that writes the reframe that adds a solve the rest of the set would miss
ranking.reason: High ambition (a trained exploration policy) and good Mac fit. But the per-task leave-one-out credit zeroes correct, different ideas (shown by arithmetic), and on 0/32 tasks training pairs will be scarce. It must first pass a Stage 0 test showing that untrained reframes crack at least 10% of tasks. PKPO narrows the novelty.

ranking.name: Prepared Mind: an open-questions board where each new win goes looking for old failures
ranking.reason: Cheap, and it fits the Mac well. But the first test as designed only measures forward retrieval (ExpeL/ReasoningBank with Jaccard), not the new reverse direction. The likely gain comes from good generic rules (the KP arm), not from matching. Worth keeping as a card-pipeline improvement, not as the creative-mode headline.

ranking.name: Night Lab: overnight read-only experiments that turn failures into verified facts about the tools
ranking.reason: Best real-use story for Ben's persistent Mac environment, and very cheap. But the failures in the readable logs are about policy and diligence (claiming done, quitting, ask/confirm), not about misunderstanding tools. Each mock world is task-local, so the cross-task library is probably empty on Reach-1, and the R+P scouting arm will likely absorb any gain. Run LAB-0 (the free audit) as a side check, and keep the real-Mac pilot.

ranking.name: Latent Escape: learned fail-to-win activation directions as branches, then an overnight checker-guided search in their span
ranking.reason: Ambitious, but two of its three failure modes are close to certain. On the same task, wins and fails share an identical prompt, so the direction encodes text the model already wrote (BORROW done in activation space). Greedy fitness is flat, so ES is about the same as random search. It is mined from mixed tasks, not from 0/64 ones. Lowest expected gain.

picks.name: Doubt Forks (DF-1'): force the runner-up at confident decision tokens, then turn the fork wins into first-try habits with fork-DPO
picks.mechanism:
WHAT IT DOES. When the assistant is stuck, it reads its own failed attempts token by token and finds the decision points where it was nearly sure (p1 >= 0.9) but a second option still had real weight (p2 >= 0.005). At each such point it takes the second option instead and lets the attempt continue from there. Overnight, every fork that rescued a task becomes a preference pair that shares the prefix up to the fork: chosen = the winning continuation from the fork, rejected = the original failed continuation from the same point. These pairs train the nightly LoRA, so the next greedy first try makes the right call at that point.
STEP BY STEP (stuck mode, K2-3.7B only):
(1) Input: the 2 failed transcripts R+ already sees.
(2) One teacher-forced prefill per transcript with top-20 logprobs (vLLM prompt_logprobs=20; on the Mac, mlx_lm logits from a single forward pass). Record p1, p2 and the entropy at every assistant token.
(3) Decision-token typing from the chat-template spans: TURN-START (the first token of an assistant turn: tool call vs final answer vs clarifying question; this covers the 'claims done after 2 turns' and 'gives up after error' failures seen in the logs), TOOL-NAME (first token of the tool name), ARG-VALUE (first token of each argument value).
(4) Candidate = decision token with p1 >= 0.9 and p2 >= 0.005.
(5) ALIAS FILTER (advisor fix): greedy-complete the span after the forced token and keep the fork only if the decoded tool name, argument value or turn type differs semantically from the original. A leading space, quote, casing or same-tool prefix counts as an alias and is dropped.
(6) Rank by log p2 plus a per-type weight. The weights are fixed in advance: TURN-START 1.0, TOOL-NAME 0.7, ARG-VALUE 0.5.
(7) Pick the top 16 forks, at most 3 per 50-token window. If fewer than 16 qualify, do not fill the shortfall with lower-quality forks: the unused budget returns to the token pool and is reported as supply shortfall.
(8) Rebuild the world by replaying the prefix's tool calls into a fresh sandbox, with a hash check of every tool output against the original. Build the prompt as transcript prefix + forced token, then sample at temp 0.7 to the 6-turn cap. vLLM prefix caching makes this cheap, and no KV truncation code is needed.
(9) Score with the task's own checks. All checks must pass to count as a success. Replay each win 3 times from the same fork.
NIGHT: fork-DPO, LoRA rank 16, beta 0.1, with the existing KL anchor and normal replay mix. It trains only on pairs from HARD-train and LOW (1-4/64) tasks. A win also becomes a playbook-card candidate ('in jobs like X, don't assume Y, do Z'), shown to Ben for confirmation. The learned probe (v1) is deferred until there are at least 30 positive fork outcomes, and it must then beat the heuristic by >=0.05 held-out AUC before it is used. One model throughout, with no second model.
picks.why_fantastic: Ben asked for truly new ways of thinking. A model cannot name an assumption it is blind to, which is why FLIP's verbal 'opposites' collapse onto ask-vs-act. Doubt Forks reads those assumptions from the model's own probabilities instead: a near-certain choice with a live alternative is mechanically a premise it never examined. That makes 'think differently' a search over its own commitments, which re-shares probability mass the model already has but judged not good enough, close to what Ben described with FlowRL/GFlowNet. More importantly, it is the only candidate that also tackles the measured bottleneck. On the puzzle model, search finds answers that greedy first-try never reproduces. A fork pair differs at exactly the token where greedy went wrong, so the DPO gradient lands on that decision and nowhere else. That is the most direct route we have from 'search found it once' to 'it gets it right first time'. It also matches the failures in the readable Reach-style logs, many of which are confident turn-start mistakes: claiming the job is done after 2 turns, or saying 'the file does not exist, let me know' and stopping. It needs no extra checks, so it works on 1- and 2-check tasks where archive and ladder ideas lack enough bits. And it compounds: every night adds fork outcomes, and the probe eventually learns which confidences are worth doubting.
picks.why_new: Not FLIP: there is no listing prompt, and the alternatives come from logprobs. Not R+ or a temperature change: specific runner-up tokens are forced at chosen points. Not the high-entropy 'forking token' work (2506.01939, Qwen 80/20): that targets uncertain tokens, while this targets confident ones, and DF-ent tests the difference head-to-head. Not PivoARL (2607.03702): there the pivot turn is chosen by self-reflection. Narrowed honestly: divergence-point DPO for tool agents already exists (2606.23112), but its pairs come from naturally diverging rollouts. Here the alternative is forced by logprob at a confident decision token and certified by the checks. 2604.22271 argues confidence alone may not localise errors, and this is the hypothesis DF-ent and DF-loc test. The citation 2412.07961 is dropped as unverified. Known-ids: 2506.01939, 2607.03702 and 2606.23112 are not in known-ids.txt and should be added. No combination of confident-token forcing + exact sandbox replay + fork-DPO on a 3-4B tool agent against matched controls was found (7 searches; suggested, not proven).
picks.prereg:
DF-1' PRE-REGISTRATION (K2-Horizon-3.7B, Reach-1 tool sandbox only; separate from the puzzle and village reports; a new PREREG file, and Reach-1's existing prereg is not edited). All pass marks below are fixed before any Step 1 episode runs.

TASKS. Shared K2 HARD screen: thinking off, temp 0.7 / top_p 0.95, 6-turn cap, 8 plain tries on the --half subset (210 tasks), then 56 more on tasks that are 0/8. HARD = 0/64. LOW = 1-4/64. If HARD on --half has fewer than 50 tasks, extend the screen to all 420. Split HARD by scenario type into HARD-test (60%, minimum 30, maximum 40 tasks) and HARD-train (40%). If HARD-test < 30, mark the run inconclusive by design and do not run Step 1.

STEP 0 (GATE; no GPU; Mac capped job or Kaggle CPU; run first). On the existing HARD and LOW failure transcripts (including the 270 paused Reach-1 episodes where they match K2), compute forks through the alias filter, and run the replay-equality hash check on 20 sampled prefixes per scenario type.
GO only if all three hold:
(G1) >=8 distinct surviving forks per task on >=70% of HARD tasks.
(G2) 100% replay equality. If any tool output contains time, random ids or order-dependent values, freeze or normalise them in the replay wrapper and re-check; if equality still fails, stop.
(G3) Every check is a deterministic end-state check, or a reply check that is re-run on the continuation.
Also report candidates per task by type, and the share of TURN-START forks.

STEP 1 (CRACKING; 2 seeds; seed = sampling RNG for every arm; fork positions are deterministic given the transcripts). Arms on HARD-test, all with the same 2 failed transcripts as context:
- R+: the existing R+ block ('try a different approach'), 16 tries, then extra tries up to the DF0 generated-token total (cap 24).
- DF0: confident forks, forced runner-up, 16 forks × 1 continuation.
- DF-ent: the 16 highest-entropy decision tokens of the same types, forced runner-up (this tests the forking-token view).
- DF-loc: DF0's exact positions, no forcing, resampled at temp 0.7 (tests whether it is the forced token or just the restart point).
- DF-randdec: random decision tokens of the same types, no confidence filter, forced runner-up.
- R+NUDGE (seed 1 only, report-only): R+ plus the one-line instruction 'before giving a final answer, check with a tool that each requested change was actually made; if a tool errors, try another route'. This is the prompt that would explain a win set dominated by stop-vs-act flips.

EQUAL COMPUTE. Every arm gets 16 tries or forks. Generated tokens are matched to DF0 within ±10%, with R+ topped up with extra tries. Prompt tokens are counted for every arm. The DF arms are charged the teacher-forced prefill of both transcripts, and cached prefix tokens are counted at full cost. Total (prompt + generated) is reported per arm. If DF0's total exceeds R+'s by more than 25%, R+ gets extra tries until the totals match, and the decisive comparison uses that total-matched R+. No arm trains in Step 1 (0 GPU steps). Wall-clock is reported on the 5070 Ti.

METRICS. Crack = all checks pass in at least one try for that task and seed. Also: cracks by fork type; supply shortfall; replay rate; per-arm tokens and wall-clock.

PASS (fixed; uses the mean of the 2 seeds unless stated otherwise):
- P1: DF0 cracks >= 5 tasks per seed on average.
- P2: DF0 − R+ >= 3, with the same sign in both seeds, and a one-sided sign test on discordant (task, seed) pairs, only-DF0 vs only-R+, with p <= 0.10.
- P3: DF0 − max(DF-ent, DF-loc, DF-randdec) >= 2, with the same sign in both seeds.
- P4: each DF0 win replays >= 2/3 from its fork.

PROVED WRONG:
- DF0 <= R+: forks add nothing over retries that see the failures.

picks.name: Impasse Forge (backup): manufacture certified stuck states from our own wins and train the creative mode to detour
picks.mechanism: Each night, take sandbox tasks the plain model solves (>=1/8). Find the load-bearing step by ablation: the first tool call whose removal makes a replay fail. Block it with one of 3 typed blocks: (a) the tool returns an error, (b) the target item is moved or renamed, (c) the argument form used is rejected and another form is needed. The 'ask' block is dropped because the sandbox has no simulated user. Error wording varies, and 20% of blocks are decoys: temporary errors where retrying the same call is correct, so 'never repeat' cannot become a reflex. Certify each impasse: a detour passes the same end-state checks, found either by the base model within 16 R+ tries (early stop) or by one Claude Batches trajectory. Claude detours only certify and are never trained on. Keep the impasse only if the plain worker fails it >=7/8. The creative adapter then writes 8 approach lines per impasse, with 1 worker try each. DPO pairs: chosen = an approach whose episode passed; rejected = an approach in the same set that re-hit the wall, defined as the same failing tool and argument signature called 2 or more times after an error. LoRA rank 16, beta 0.1, KL anchor. At serve time it is an ordinary creative call.
picks.why_fantastic: It turns the scarcest thing, examples of getting unstuck, into something the system makes every night from its own wins, with ground truth. A 0/64 task gives zero signal, and this sidesteps that without hindsight relabelling (the goal stays fixed and only the route is broken). If it transfers, the assistant gets better at recovering from new failures without Ben having to fail first. The readable logs include exactly this kind of failure, for example 'the file does not exist, let me know' after 2 turns on error_recovery tasks.
picks.why_new: Fission-GRPO (2601.15625) trains recovery from errors made by an error simulator. Forge instead blocks the step found by ablation, certifies that a detour exists, retires and stacks blocks as a curriculum, and trains a separate exploration mode with 're-hit the wall' negatives. ToolMaze (2606.05806) only benchmarks injected failures. AgentHER, ECHO and HSL change the goal, not the route. Novelty rests on beating Fission-style random-block training (P3).

judged.plain_summary:
Ben, here's the short version. We had eight ideas for the 'creative mode', the part of the assistant that switches on when it's stuck. I ranked them, and the winner is called Doubt Forks.

The idea: when the assistant fails, look back through its failed attempt for the spots where it was 'pretty sure, but not totally sure' about a choice. Examples are deciding the job was done, giving up after an error, or picking which tool to use. At each of those spots we make it take its second choice and see if that rescues the task. Then, overnight, we train on the exact spot where the second choice won, so next time it gets it right on the first try. Getting it right first time is the thing our earlier experiments kept failing at. Search would find an answer once, and the normal first try would never repeat it.

Why this one: it goes after that known weak point directly. It's cheap, and it runs on your Mac. It also fits what the logs show: many of the failures are the model saying 'done!' too early, or quitting after one error.

How we keep it honest:
- First, a free check with no GPU: are there enough of these 'pretty sure' spots in its failures, and does the sandbox replay exactly?
- Then a fair race, run twice. It goes against ordinary retries that see the failures, and against three look-alike versions: forcing the second choice where the model was unsure, restarting from the same spot without forcing anything, and forcing at random decision points. Every version gets the same number of tries and tokens.
- If Doubt Forks doesn't beat all of them by the margins we wrote down in advance, the idea is wrong, and we say so.
- Only if it wins do we try the overnight training. We test that on tasks it never trained on, so it can't just memorise answers.

The whole first test fits in about 6-7 hours on your PC plus the second Kaggle account. No paid compute.

The backup is Impasse Forge. It deliberately breaks things that already worked so the assistant can practise finding a way around, and it only runs if a cheap $2 check shows your hard tasks really fail that way.

I dropped the 'archive of partial wins' idea from the top spot for one reason: each task only has about 2 checks, so there isn't enough partial-credit information for it to work with.
